article_title: The UK haemophilia specialist nurse: Competencies fit for practice in the 21st century.
citation: Pollard D, Harrison C, Dodgson S, Holland M, Khair K. (2020). The UK haemophilia specialist nurse: Competencies fit for practice in the 21st century. Haemophilia. https://doi.org/10.1111/hae.14002
title: HNA five-domain competency framework for haemophilia specialist nurses with four levels of practice
description: The UK Haemophilia Nurses Association competency framework organises haemophilia specialist nursing competence into five domains — clinical knowledge, clinical/direct care, communication and support, collaborative practice, and research — "supported by indicators for four levels of practice (beginner, competent, proficient and expert)". Each level's indicators provide a standard against which nurses can measure their personal practice, developed through three regional workshops with 66 nurses and consensus ranking of competence against time in practice. It updates the 2014 framework within Health Education England's multiprofessional advanced clinical practice structure.
requirements: Nurses and their managers use the framework to assess existing skills and knowledge and identify learning needs appropriate to personal development
constraints: The indicative timeframes for progressing between levels should be interpreted cautiously because the rate at which nurses gain experience depends on the level of clinical activity in their centre, prior roles and skill transferability
target_learners: UK haemophilia specialist nurses from beginner to expert level
examples: Tables 1–5 print indicators for each domain at each of the four levels, e.g. level 1 clinical knowledge includes understanding the variety of bleeding disorders and their hereditary nature; level 4 includes prescribing replacement therapy in line with qualification.
key_sources: Pollard D, Harrison C, Dodgson S, Holland M, Khair K. (2020). The UK haemophilia specialist nurse: Competencies fit for practice in the 21st century. Haemophilia. https://doi.org/10.1111/hae.14002

article_title: [Communication training in otorhinolaryngology education : Comparison of an online and a classroom-based training course].
citation: Gür Deniz, Offergeld Christian, Fabry Götz, Wünsch Alexander. (2024). Vermittlung kommunikativer Kompetenzen in der Lehre der HNO-Heilkunde: Vergleich zwischen einer Online- und Präsenzveranstaltung. HNO. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00106-024-01475-2
title: Blended-structure communication training unit: asynchronous video preparation plus synchronous simulated-patient consultations in videoconference break-out rooms with layered feedback
description: The intervention consists of an asynchronous preparation video on communicative competences and audiology (causes of hearing disorders, cochlear implant indications, speech audiogram interpretation), followed by synchronous small-group work in videoconference break-out rooms where pairs of students conduct consultations with a simulated patient portraying a hearing-impaired person. Observer tasks based on the COM-ON-Check and NURSE models structure peer feedback, followed by self-reflection and feedback from the simulated patient and tutor. The article describes it as "in Aufbau und Dauer vergleichbar" to the prior face-to-face event, with a conversation of about 15 minutes and a feedback round of about 15 minutes.
requirements: A platform for videoconferences with break-out rooms
A simulated patient and a tutor assigned to each small group
A central learning platform hosting the preparation videos
constraints: The online version was voluntary attendance whereas the face-to-face version was mandatory, a difference the article names
Technical disruptions were reported by students
Nonverbal aspects were harder to evaluate online
target_learners: Medical students in the otolaryngology block practicum, third and fourth clinical semester
target_learning_goals: Communication skills for consultations with hearing-impaired patients, including history taking, explaining findings, and counselling about diagnosis and treatment
examples: The case used was a patient who had suffered sudden hearing loss and for whom a cochlear implant was recommended
key_sources: Gür Deniz, Offergeld Christian, Fabry Götz, Wünsch Alexander. (2024). Vermittlung kommunikativer Kompetenzen in der Lehre der HNO-Heilkunde: Vergleich zwischen einer Online- und Präsenzveranstaltung. HNO. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00106-024-01475-2

article_title: Newspaper Reading in Families with School-Age Children: Relationship between Parent-Child Interaction Using Newspaper, Reading Motivation, and Academic Achievement.
citation: Choi Naya, Sheo Jiyeon, Jung Suji, Choi Jisu. (2022). Newspaper Reading in Families with School-Age Children: Relationship between Parent–Child Interaction Using Newspaper, Reading Motivation, and Academic Achievement. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, 19(21), 14423. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph192114423
title: Home Newspaper Utilization Scale for Elementary School Students (HNUS-E), Activities factor
description: The HNUS-E, developed by Choi and Jeong, is a parent-report instrument measuring parent–child interactional behaviors using newspapers. The article uses only its 'Activities' factor, which "consists of 18 items and 4 subfactors": play activity, conversation, online mediation, and scrap activity, each rated on a 5-point Likert scale. Subfactor Cronbach's α values printed in the article are 0.96 (play), 0.97 (conversation), 0.96 (online mediation), and 0.94 (scrap activity). The full scale is described as covering 3 factors and 9 subfactors, and it is one of the few scales including online interaction with newspapers.
requirements: Respondents are parents reporting on their own interactional behaviors with their child using newspapers, on 5-point Likert items.
constraints: Only the 'Activities' factor was used in this study because the majority of interactional activities require the physical presence of newspapers.
target_learning_goals: Home literacy environment and parent–child literacy interaction
examples: Sample items include "I play games using newspapers with my child" (play activity) and "I discuss newspaper articles with my child after reading together" (conversation).
key_sources: Choi Naya, Sheo Jiyeon, Jung Suji, Choi Jisu. (2022). Newspaper Reading in Families with School-Age Children: Relationship between Parent–Child Interaction Using Newspaper, Reading Motivation, and Academic Achievement. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, 19(21), 14423. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph192114423
